topic: The Twitter Collapse: From Reign to Rebuild
description: A high-contrast timeline of how X (Twitter) cratered in ad demand and valuation after leadership shocks—and how it later tried to stabilize. Built for a chart-race-style video with real milestone anchors from 2022–2025.

⏱️ Timeline Comparison: “The Twitter Collapse: From Reign to Rebuild”

In this video, we chart how the ad-money gravity shifted after Twitter’s acquisition shock and the following years of instability—while Meta and Google re-captured attention and advertising spend at scale.

CHAPTERS
0:00 — The setup: Twitter’s 2022 inflection
0:18 — Valuation shock: X declines fast post-deal
0:45 — 2023: advertisers re-price risk, Meta keeps scaling
1:20 — 2024: platforms diversify ad formats; X struggles
1:55 — 2025: attempted stabilization vs continued drawdown
2:20 — Chart-race wrap-up: who wins the ad market while the timelines break

What you’ll see: one platform’s value collapses while others keep compounding—even when the wider economy tightens.

Engage: Which segment do you think matters more for platform survival—ad revenue durability, user trust, or creator flywheels?

instagram_caption:
🚨 The $44B → ~$12B collapse: what happened to X (Twitter) as Meta & Google swallowed the ad market?

Picture this: in late 2022, X is still trying to find its footing after the biggest leadership and strategy shock in its history. But the market didn’t wait for a “new plan.” It priced in uncertainty—fast. In our timeline, X’s valuation starts at about $44B in 2022, then slides to ~$18B in 2023 and down again to ~$11B in 2024. By 2025, it’s still not back—hovering around ~$12B.

Meanwhile, the ad economy didn’t freeze. It just moved.
In 2022, Meta sits around $1.19T in valuation, while Alphabet is about $213B. Both platforms kept leaning into the feedback loop advertisers love: targeting + measurable performance + massive scale.
Then 2023 hits and Meta climbs to roughly $1.65T while Alphabet rises to about $238B. Even with macro pressure, those platforms remained the “default” choices for brand spend.

By 2024, Meta is ~ $1.81T and Alphabet is ~ $281B. That year matters because X wasn’t just fighting for revenue—it was fighting for trust and consistency. Ad ecosystems reward predictability. When it’s missing, budgets don’t sit still. Snap, meanwhile, also drops hard from ~$25B (2022) to ~$7B (2023), then stabilizes around ~$9–$10B into 2024–2025.

The dramatic part of this chart race: X loses its gravitational pull, while Meta and Alphabet keep compounding. It’s not just a “Twitter vs others” story—it’s a market-structure story about where advertising confidence goes when a platform’s trajectory becomes unclear.

💬 Question for you: If you were an advertiser in 2023, would you chase X for “potential upside,” or buy into Meta/Google for “proven returns”?

facebook_caption:
X (formerly Twitter) didn’t just change leadership—it experienced a valuation reset that played out across the ad market. In 2022, X is modeled at roughly $44B. By 2023, its valuation drops to about $18B as advertisers and investors re-assess risk and monetization reliability. The decline continues through 2024 to about $11B, and although 2025 shows slight stabilization (~$12B), the recovery is incomplete.

While X struggled, competing ad ecosystems expanded. Meta’s valuation rises from about $1.19T (2022) to about $1.65T (2023) and about $1.81T (2024). Alphabet similarly grows from about $213B (2022) to about $238B (2023) and about $281B (2024), reflecting durable demand and performance-driven advertising infrastructure.

This creates the chart-race contrast: as X loses market confidence, Meta and Alphabet compound, and Snap—already pressured—remains far smaller, hovering around ~$7–$10B into 2025.
